D009-D018_h001.question:
I’ve been struggling for about a year now—some months are worse than others. There are times when I feel like I’m running on a treadmill at full speed. I’ll start three projects at work at once, call clients late at night, barely sleep—sometimes just two or three hours—but I don’t feel tired. My thoughts race, and I can’t stop talking, even if people look uncomfortable. I pace during calls, fidget with pens, can’t sit still. Then, just as suddenly, it fades.  

But more often, I’m just… empty. Getting out of bed takes everything. I’ve started crying at work—quietly, in the bathroom—over nothing. I stare at my computer and can’t focus. My mind feels like it’s drowning in thick fog. The motivation’s gone. I think, “What’s the point?” Sometimes I even think it would be easier if I weren’t here—no plan, just… a wish.  

A while back, something terrible happened—personal, but I don’t like to talk about it. It shook me. But these mood swings—they don’t always line up with memories of it. Sometimes I’m up when I should be down, irritable when I’ve had no trigger. It’s all jumbled. Like my nervous system doesn’t know whether to flee, fight, or collapse.
D009-D018_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder
D009-D018_h001.answer: B & A. Bipolar II Disorder & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D009-D018_h002.question:

D009-D018_h022.question:
I’ve been feeling… off… for over a year now. Some days, I’m running on three hours of sleep and it doesn’t even faze me—I’ll go home after a 12-hour shift and start tearing apart the garage, like I’ve got to *do* something, anything. I don’t feel tired, just wired. But then, it flips. I can’t enjoy things—not cooking, not hanging out with my wife, nothing. I just sit there, restless, shaking my leg, pulling at my nails until they bleed. I feel heavy, even when I’m moving.  

The sadness sticks. It’s like a fog I can’t burn through. I used to love the rush of the kitchen, the heat, the noise—but now it all just grates. I snap at my line cooks over small mistakes. I don’t know if it’s stress or what, but sometimes I wonder if it’s because of that night last year—the accident. I was driving. No one died, but… it was bad. I don’t know if I’ve ever talked about it properly. I don’t dream about it much, but sometimes I feel amped up for no reason, like I’m waiting for something to go wrong.  

It’s not like I can’t work—I’m still holding it together at the restaurant—but at home, I’m worn out. Even when I sleep, I feel exhausted.
